newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: COCOA--Ghana 96/97 season opens Friday, price held.
newsitem.headline: COCOA--Ghana 96/97 season opens Friday, price held.

text.p: Ghana set its 1996/97 cocoa marketing season from Friday with producer prices unchanged from the start of the light crop in June.
The Ghana News Agency said late on Tuesday Ghana's state cocoa marketing board (Cocobod) had set a rate of 36,000 cedis per 30 kg for a load of grade one and two naked ex-scale.
It also fixed a price of 75,000 cedis per 60 kg bag, or 1.2 million for 16 bags, effective at all Ghana buying stations.

One Abidjan crop analyst said the new price was a blow to producers as the rate was the same as the 1,200 cedis per kg set in June. "The new price works out the same but the cedi has devalued since May. The farmer will see a real loss," he said.

Ghana's official 1995/96 production was put at 400,000 tonnes by Finance Minister Kwame Peprah in September, while London trader ED & F Man in September estimated the total 1995/96 crop at around 390,000 tonnes.
Ghana's cocoa is widely regarded as the best quality available and often attracts a 30 stg per tonne premium over terminal prices. Many other origins sell at a discount.
Forecasters expect Ghana's 1996/97 total crop to be affected by poor pod-setting following July and August rains and later evidence of blackpod in September.
At 1,200 cedi per kg the new price is equal to about 366 CFA per kg, above the current 315 CFA set last October by Ivory Coast, the world's top producer, for its 1995/96 season.
Ivory Coast is due to open its 1996/97 cocoa campaign on October 15 with the farmgate price expected by analysts to be unchanged or up slightly. It will now face pressure to opt for a rise, said one.
"The difference in price could put pressure on Ivory Coast to raise its prices to producers to prevent an increase in smuggling," he said.
International Monetary Fund "illustrative calculations" earlier this year suggested Ivory Coast could set a 360 CFA per kg rate for 1996/97, more in line with Ghana's price.

Others said Ghana's superior cocoa quality justified its current premium. In August, a senior Ghanaian cocoa official said Ghana must keep up-country cocoa quality checks in place despite donor-backed moves to streamline the sector because they cost less than the sales premium they safeguard.
Ivory Coast's Caistab marketing agency closed its up-country testing centres last year as part of a $150 million World Bank loan deal.
Ghana raised its farmgate cocoa price to 1,200 cedis from 840 cedis at the start of the mid-crop season on June 7.
An outbreak of blackpod disease in September hit cocoa in Ghana's Brong Ahafo region, where about 12 percent of the country's crop is grown, according to official reports in Ghana at the time.
There was concern among farmers who foresaw a loss of income in the pending main season.
Blackpod is a fungal disease that attacks pods and rots the beans inside. It is controlled by use of copper-based chemicals.
Its spread was hastened this year by late delivery of chemicals to producers following changes to the distribution network by farmers' leaders, said officials.
